f.title: Treat any untoward medical occurrence with drug use as an adverse event, including with active control or placebo
f.statement: Adverse event means any untoward medical occurrence associated with the use of a drug in humans, whether or not considered drug related (21 CFR 312.32(a)). FDA considers an adverse event (also referred to as an adverse experience) to include any unfavorable sign (e.g., an abnormal laboratory finding), symptom, or clinical outcome temporally associated with the use of an investigational drug, an active control, or a placebo, regardless of whether the event is thought to be related to the drug. An adverse event can arise during any use of a drug (e.g., use for a purpose other than the FDA-approved indication or in combination with another drug) and with any route of administration, formulation, or dose, including an overdose.

Suspected adverse reaction implies a lesser degree of certainty about causality than adverse reaction (21 CFR 312.32(a)).

f.title: Report study endpoints per protocol, not as IND safety reports unless causal evidence exists

For example, in an all-cause mortality trial a death would ordinarily not be reported individually, but a death resulting from an anaphylactic reaction coinciding with initial exposure or from fatal hepatic necrosis must be reported as an individual case in an IND safety report.

If the overall blinded analyses show that the rate in the pooled treatment groups is notably higher (exceeding the predicted rate by more than a minor difference and meeting the unblinding criteria), the next step would be an unblinded analysis comparing the numbers of events in each arm to determine whether the criteria in 21 CFR 312.32(c)(1)(i)(C) have been met. Clinical judgment should be incorporated into any assessment, because some circumstances may mitigate the need for unblinding even if a trigger rate is exceeded.
f.clause: VI.C.1.b. Unblinding trigger approach
f.processes: Clinical safety monitoring; Signal detection; Reporting policy

Note that clinical judgment should be incorporated into any assessment because there may be circumstances that mitigate the need for unblinding even if a trigger rate is exceeded.

f.title: Base unblinding triggers on probability and clinical judgment when rate data are limited
f.statement: For anticipated SAEs with limited or no available rate data for the study population, the trigger for unblinding may be based on statistical probability and clinical judgment. For example, unblinding should be done if there are more than a few SAEs of a certain type such that, if most occurred in the investigational arm, one would suspect a causal role. Such a trigger should be set based on review of blinded data for anticipated events that do not occur frequently and have not been prespecified.
